title: Never Say Yes Unless You Mean It
intro: The Mufaddaliyyat transmits counsels on keeping one’s word together with verses for Khalid, who secured the release of the poet’s nephew Sha’s. Al-Marzuqi records a tradition assigning the opening to another poet of Abd al-Qays and the praise of Khalid to al-Muthaqqib. In this performance, ordinary exchanges of yes and no lead to the question of what a man will spend to keep faith.

translation: Never say, when you have no intention
of keeping a promise in some matter, “Yes.”
1.sharh: The word being forbidden arrives last. By the time “yes” is heard, the speaker has made the listener consider everything that one syllable undertakes.

translation: A “yes” spoken after “no” is gracious.
How ugly a “no” after “yes.”
2.sharh: The words exchange places across the caesura. A refusal can still be reopened, whereas withdrawing an assent deprives someone of what they have begun to count on.

translation: To say “no” after “yes” is an outrage.
Begin with “no” if you fear regret.
3.sharh: His test is practical. Someone who already foresees regret can spare the petitioner both a wait and a second, more painful answer.

translation: Once you have said “yes,” stand by it
and make the word good. To break it is disgrace.
4.sharh: Patience here is the work of carrying out an undertaking. The word only succeeds when something actually reaches the person to whom it was given.

translation: Know that blame diminishes a man.
Whoever fails to guard against blame earns it.
5.sharh: The same Arabic root supplies the risk and the verdict. A reputation rests partly in other people’s mouths, but his conduct gives them their grounds.

translation: I honour the man under my protection and keep his rights.
For a man to recognize a rightful claim is nobility.
6.sharh: The neighbour can be an outsider who has entered under a man’s protection. His host’s generosity begins in acknowledging an obligation the weaker party can already claim.

translation: You will never see me feeding at ease in a gathering
on human flesh, like a ravenous beast.
7.sharh: Backbiting becomes a meal. The ease with which a beast feeds makes the social ease of the gossiping circle particularly disturbing.

translation: The worst of men bares his teeth in a smile
when he meets me, and reviles me when I leave.
8.sharh: Bared teeth now pass for a friendly smile. The movement links this man to the feeding animal of the previous verse before the abuse behind the smile is disclosed.

translation: Many an ugly word my ear has been deaf to,
though there is nothing wrong with my hearing.
9.sharh: He distinguishes the ear’s physical ability from the listener’s response. Acting deaf stops an insult from gaining a second voice or a wider audience.

translation: I held myself in, for fear a fool might think
I really was the man he claimed I was.
10.sharh: An angry reply might supply the fool with the very likeness his slander invented. The speaker refuses to perform the character someone else has written for him.

translation: Some things last better if one forgives and turns away
from a foul-mouthed man, even when he has done wrong.
11.sharh: “Some” leaves room for judgment. A wrong can be real even when pursuing it would cost more of a relationship or a reputation than letting it go.

translation: Khalid was generous indeed in the matter of Sha’s
after one of the dark calamities had closed around him,
12.sharh: Sha’s is the captive whose release Khalid obtained. The poem measures the gift from the captive’s position, when he could see no way to extricate himself.

translation: one of the deaths that played odd and even with him,
each racing for this body of flesh and blood.
13.sharh: The deaths gamble over him as children guess odd or even. The ordinary materials of a living body make the stake in their game uncomfortably tangible.

translation: His serving bowl is brimful, his bounty strong as spring growth.
His gatherings are gracious, with no striking of faces.
14.sharh: The spring image evokes a calf born while its dam still has abundant pasture. The generous host also attends to the weaker visitor’s dignity once he is seated.

translation: He makes his gifts a great abundance.
Some wealth is a small price to pay for honour.
15.sharh: The gifts look large from the recipient’s side of the exchange. Set against the honour secured by giving them, the same outlay falls within reasonable bounds.

translation: His heart is easy. It costs him no concern
to lose his property when his honour is safe.
16.sharh: At the close, the loss has actually taken place. Khalid’s contentment makes good the opening promise that the worth of a word is known when the bill comes due.

3.1.5.head: فاحِشَة
3.1.5.meaning: An act of gross impropriety, here reneging after giving assent.

4.2.1-2.head: نَجاح القَول
4.2.1-2.meaning: Making a word succeed by delivering what it promised.

6.1.2.head: الجار
6.1.2.meaning: A person sheltered by another’s pledge of protection.

7.1.3.head: راتِع
7.1.3.meaning: Feeding at liberty, originally of animals at pasture.

8.1.5.head: كَشَرَ
8.1.5.meaning: To draw back the lips and show the teeth, here in a smile.

9.1.4.meaning: To be stopped or made heavy of hearing.

10.1.1.head: تَعَزّى
10.1.1.meaning: To master oneself and bear a hurt.

12.1.3.head: شَأس
12.1.3.meaning: Sha’s ibn Nahar, al-Muthaqqib’s sister’s son, himself a poet known as al-Mumazzaq.

12.1.4.head: خالِد
12.1.4.meaning: Khalid, identified in one account as Khalid ibn al-Harith, the captive’s intercessor.

13.1.3.head: تَخاسى
13.1.3.meaning: To play at guessing odd and even, with odd called khasa.

14.1.1-2.head: مُترَع الجَفنَة
14.1.1-2.meaning: One whose large serving bowl is filled to the brim.

14.1.3-4.head: رِبعِيّ النَّدى
14.1.3-4.meaning: Bounteous like the early spring yield, originally of a calf born early in the season.

14.2.4.meaning: Blows to the face, a humiliation absent from his gathering.

15.1.2.head: الهَنء
15.1.2.meaning: A gift or the act of bestowing one.

15.2.6.meaning: A reasonable measure or a light cost, reckoned against honour.

16.2.4.head: العِرض
16.2.4.meaning: The honour and good name exposed to praise or blame.

5.1.1.head: اِعلَم
5.1.1.meaning: Know. In connected speech the vowel of the following particle can move back onto the final consonant of the imperative.

12.2.3.head: حاقَ
12.2.3.meaning: To settle upon and encompass someone, here of an ordeal.

16.1.3-4.head: طَيِّب النَّفس
16.1.3-4.meaning: “At ease in his mind” about the expenditure. The card gives a nominative description and also records the accusative, “being content”, printed by Shakir and Harun.
